.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 222 PM EDT Tuesday...

A Flood Watch has been issued for much of central/southern Vermont 
and Essex County NY. Expected rainfall in those areas has increased. 
Amounts between 2-3 inches should fall in most places, with isolated 
amounts up to 5 inches possible. Isolated to scattered flash 
flooding is possible there.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 222 PM EDT Tuesday...

1. Periods of rain continue tonight through Wednesday night.
Localized flash flooding is possible if storms repeatedly track over 
the same area. 

2. After a brief period of drier weather, unsettled conditions 
are expected to return later this weekend into the beginning of next 
week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 222 PM EDT Tuesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: An upper-level low builds into the region today and 
remains over the area into Thursday. An associated surface low has 
formed over the Great Lakes and it will occlude as it moves into New 
York and New England, bringing consistent showers. The widespread 
showers have entered northern New York, and scattered showers and 
thunderstorms have developed across the higher terrain in Vermont. 
As the afternoon and evening progress, the combination of 
strengthening synoptic dynamics and increasing instability will 
cause these showers to become widespread. A lack of deep-layer is 
expected to prevent any severe threat though. These storms will 
likely have the highest rainfall rates of the entire event, but dry 
antecedent conditions and some south to north storm motion should 
keep the flood threat relatively low through this afternoon. The 
axis of rain will become more sse-nnw oriented heading into this 
evening and night, and mostly stall in the same locations. However, 
as the evening goes on, this axis of rain looks to become a more 
broken line, so there will be rounds of showers heading over 
the areas but likely not constant rain. While the precipitation 
should trend toward more stratiform as the night goes on, some 
convective enhancement will still be likely, especially in 
southern Vermont where the highest totals are expected. This 
Tuesday night into Wednesday morning would likely have the 
highest concern for any flash flooding as the axis of rain looks
to stay relatively stationary. Heading through tomorrow, the 
dynamics weaken and the axis of rain looks to become more broken
and lighter. Periods of showers will continue tomorrow night 
through Thursday, but they will become much lighter and 
gradually less widespread as the surface low weakens and pushes 
east. The area of highest concern is the eastern slopes and 
spine of the southern Green Mountains where the best dynamics 
will combine with upsloping. The east slopes of the Adirondacks 
will likely be the second area of focus due to the upsloping. 
Most areas will see between 1-3 inches of rain, but isolated 
areas up to 5 inches are possible in parts of the southern 
Greens. Still, in the more favored areas, only isolated to 
scattered flash flooding looks to be possible. The Champlain 
Valley and Northeast Kingdom will likely receive some locally 
lower totals due to downsloping. Showers will become much more 
isolated heading into Friday.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Brief ridging across the region will continue to bring 
drier conditions for the start of the weekend. Seasonably warm 
temperatures are expected for the start of this weekend, with high 
temperatures in 80s areawide. Unsettled weather conditions are 
expected to return for the latter half of the weekend into the 
beginning of next week as another shortwave trough moves through, 
although there is still some uncertainty regarding the timing of 
this feature and how widespread showers will be. Temperatures will 
largely be influenced by any cloud cover and precipitation, but 
above normal temperatures are anticipated with highs climbing into 
the mid 70s and 80s with overnight lows in the upper 50s and 60s.

&&

.AVIATION /00Z WEDNESDAY THROUGH SUNDAY/...
Through 00Z Thursday...Rain and a few rumbles of thunder are
lifting north across the region. A few downpours have dropped 
visibilities below 3SM, but the extent of heavy rain has been
diminishing. Upcoming activity is not expected to have much
lightning, and no explicit mention of thunder is noted for any
TAF, but could occur through 06z and again after 13z Wednesday.
Favored a gradual reduction in ceilings and visibility with the
potential for the worst surface conditions around 09z-17z with 
most terminals IFR or near-IFR. This will be timed with heavy 
rain associated with a surface low expected to pass north. Winds
will go calm or variable on its approach. Southeast winds will 
then be favored across Vermont, and northeast over northern New 
York with speeds increasing to 6-11 knots sustained, with some 
downslope gusting at areas like KRUT up to 20-22 knots. 
Eventually, low pressure will develop more strongly off the New 
England Coast. Surface winds will begin to diminish, but the 
flow aloft will remain southeasterly at 30-40 knots at 2000 ft 
agl across Vermont. Some LLWS is noted. As the surface low 
decays, conditions are expected to improve. However, across 
Vermont, there will likely be some redeveloping convection 18z 
Wed to about 03z Thurs, which could produce locally heavy rain 
reducing visibilities.

Outlook...

Wednesday Night: Mainly VFR, with local IFR possible. Chance
SHRA.
Thursday: Mainly MVFR, with local IFR possible. Chance SHRA,
Slight chance TSRA.
Thursday Night: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. NO SIG WX.
Friday: VFR. Slight chance SHRA.
Friday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Saturday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Saturday Night: VFR. Slight chance SHRA.
Sunday: VFR. Chance SHRA, Chance TSRA.

&&

NY...Flood Watch through Wednesday evening for NYZ034-035.

&&
